plants.name: Prunus mume
plants.description: A small deciduous tree that produces fragrant five-petaled blossoms on bare branches in late winter, often while snow is still on the ground. It is widely cultivated in Japan, China, and Korea, and its flowers are a traditional symbol of perseverance and the coming of spring.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late winter to early spring (January to March)
plants.location: East Asia (Japan, China, Korea); cultivated in temperate gardens worldwide
plants.funFact: Ume blossoms are celebrated in Japan with ume matsuri festivals, and the fruit is pickled to make umeboshi and also used to make plum wine.

plants.name: Galanthus nivalis
plants.description: A small bulbous perennial with drooping, bell-shaped white flowers marked with green on the inner petals. It pushes up through frost and snow in woodlands and gardens, and often forms large carpets in naturalized areas.
plants.location: Europe, from the Pyrenees to Ukraine; naturalized in the UK and North America
plants.funFact: Snowdrops produce a compound called galantamine, which is used in medicine to treat symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: A striking evergreen shrub with the largest flower head in the Protea genus, made up of a central cone surrounded by showy pink bracts. It thrives in the fynbos vegetation of the Cape region, where it is adapted to nutrient-poor soils and periodic fires.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late summer to early spring in the Southern Hemisphere, with peak bloom in spring and some flowering in February
plants.funFact: The king protea is South Africa's national flower, and its thick underground stem lets it resprout after fires.

plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: An evergreen shrub or small tree with glossy dark green leaves and rose-like flowers that bloom in the cooler months. It is a favorite in the gardens of the southeastern United States, Japan, and the mild maritime climates of Europe and the Pacific Northwest.
plants.bloomingSeason: Winter to early spring (December to April)
plants.location: Japan, Korea, and China; widely cultivated in the southeastern USA, Europe, and Australia
plants.funFact: Camellia japonica is related to Camellia sinensis, the plant that gives us tea, and there are thousands of registered cultivars.
